summary: The mechanism is plausible and the result can be read without companions: every changed row pairs with a non-incumbent pick in the prepare() table, and keys that keep the incumbent stay byte-identical. The expected headline gain (~+0.5-1%) is below run drift, so judge it on the per-shape nvjet rows. Claim it only after the bf16 precedent 26a8be34a5eb4426 harvests: it was dispatched at 16:48Z and has no result yet, so the 'check its harvest' gate in the Risk section cannot be met at review time.
justification: Plausible on H200 for these shapes, but the profile evidence is weaker than the body says. (1) The turn_1 premise is overstated. In master's profile (fb1e52d2119d4175, archive/experts-hybrid-marlin-turn-triton-first-turn/fb1e52d2119d4175.profile.txt), nvjet_sm90_tst_128x192 at 154.0 us is 3 calls: qkv_gate, pooler and unpooler, all with K large and all TNN. Their combined floor at T=753 is 28.7 + 51.1 + 51.1 = ~131 us, so the three together already run at ~85% of peak. Pooler and unpooler alone need >=51 us each, which leaves at most ~50 us for qkv_gate against its 28.7 us floor. A 72-CTA grid costs qkv_gate perhaps 10-20 us, and the GPU is not 'half idle for the whole kernel'. The o projection is the real outlier: 39 us for one call against a 12.8 us compute floor. With K=1024 there are only 16 k-steps of 64, so prologue and epilogue dominate, and 438 CTAs make 3.3 waves. Split-K and stream-K candidates could save 10-20 us there. Turn_1 headroom is therefore ~20-35 us across 4 GEMMs of a 1080-1420 us shape, so 1-2% per turn_1 shape is a fair upper estimate. (2) turn_4 checks out: the four nvjet rows sum to ~725 us against a 574 us floor (115 qkv + 51 o + 204 pooler + 204 unpooler at T=3012), ~79% of peak. A 5-10% better tile on the two 256x152 TNT calls or the 128x256 call is 15-50 us of 3335-4938 us. (3) first_turn: the dense GEMMs are 3865 us against a ~3127 us floor (~81%). 'Flat' is the right expectation, and the 3% keep rule should hold the incumbent there. (4) Headline arithmetic: each load counts once in the geomean. +1-2% on turn_1 and +0.5-1.5% on turn_4 gives about +0.5-1.1% on the headline, inside the ~1.5-2.5% per-run drift (LESSONS). One scored run cannot resolve the headline. It is judged by the prepare() table plus the per-shape nvjet rows, as the spec already says. Weakest link: whether cublasLtMatmulAlgoGetHeuristic returns anything for this TN descriptor at M=753/3012 that is materially different from heuristic 0. bf16-cublaslt-backend-toggle showed that the backend preference alone changes nothing. The only evidence that better configs exist is the NN-layout probe at m=128, a different M and layout. The precedent that would answer this (26a8be34a5eb4426, m=128/256) has not harvested. Second weakest link: prepare() times each GEMM alone with every operand cold. In the real graph the pooler shares the GPU with the side-stream router (tss_64x96 split-K, 30.6-79.9 us for 2 calls at turn_1, 129.8-137.0 us at turn_4). The o, pooler and unpooler inputs are also L2-warm outputs of the previous kernel. A pooler pick that wins by 3-5% alone, for example by adding CTAs or split-K, can lose that margin when it contends with the router for SMs. One factual error in the spec: 'every T outside the three exact values (all 5 tests)' is wrong. Test 2 (batch 1, ctx 3000, full, q_len 753) has T=753 and will take the Lt path when a turn_1 key is chosen. That is harmless, and it means the Lt path gets correctness-tested, but the implementer should not assume the tests avoid it.
confounders: sglang-pipeline-parity: it puts the router (two torch.mm calls, fp32 out) on a side stream that overlaps the pooler GEMM. A pooler candidate picked by timing it alone can perform differently under that overlap, so a pooler-row change at turn_1 or turn_4 is partly an interaction with the side-stream layout, not a pure algorithm effect. Mitigation in the build, not a companion: time the pooler keys with the router's two mm calls replayed on the side stream inside the same captured graph, or require a larger margin (>=5%) for the pooler keys. qkv_gate, o and unpooler do not overlap anything, so they are unaffected.

experts-hybrid-marlin-turn-triton-first-turn / experts-triton-w4a16-first-turn-blockt256: no confound on the dense GEMMs. The expert kernels run strictly between pooler and unpooler on the main stream, share no buffers with the dense weights, and the experts' gains/losses live in rows (Marlin at T<=4096, _moe_nvfp4_gemm_kernel above) that this change does not touch. The one indirect effect: the unpooler's input is the expert output, L2-warm in the graph but cold in prepare() timing. That is a small bias, the same for every candidate. Prepare memory: the second expert bank (+0.9 GiB) plus up to 12 x 32 MiB of workspaces is still far from the H200 limit.
interference: No companion is warranted. A gain or a loss is attributable on its own. Each changed (layer, T) key prints its chosen algorithm (tile, stages, splitK, waves) and the prepare() timing, and each changed shape row shows a different nvjet/cutlass kernel name in top_kernels. Keys that keep the incumbent run master's byte-identical _bf16_gemm_dispatch_impl. An ab-revert of a landed hypothesis does not make sense: sglang-pipeline-parity is the whole pipeline, and the expert stages are disjoint from the dense GEMMs. The pooler/router overlap is better handled in the build (time the pooler under overlap, or use a stricter threshold) than with an extra run. The one control I considered was the Lt wrapper replaying heuristic 0, to separate wrapper overhead from algorithm choice. It is moot: the wrapper only replaces a key after it beat the incumbent by >=3% in a graph-replay timing that includes the wrapper. Prefill checks are also spent, so every run is a scored submit, which argues further against an extra run.
rules_flags: load_inline invokes the host compiler (ninja/g++) during import or prepare(). The rules reject a submission that 'starts processes'. Precedent: muse_attention_decode full-decode-cuda-gather-splitkv compiled a load_inline module at import in 41 s and was accepted. Low risk, but keep the module cpp-only, as in the bf16 impl a77cdec, and print the compile time.

_lt_route_ok checks 256-byte alignment of data_ptr(). That is a host-side branch on pointer addresses at capture time, not on input values, so it is allowed. It also means a graph captured on a misaligned buffer silently falls back to master's path. Print which path each key took during the first (uncaptured) call so the result can be read.

Precision is unchanged (bf16 in, fp32 compute, bf16 out). Split-K candidates must keep reductionScheme in COMPUTE_TYPE (fp32) or none. The spec already excludes the others; also exclude CUBLASLT_REDUCTION_SCHEME_OUTPUT_TYPE explicitly.

Nothing derived from data is cached: the algorithm is chosen from weight shapes and synthetic randn inputs inside untimed prepare(), and kernel_fn branches only on x.shape[0] (tokens), which is allowed.

Each workspace must belong to exactly one key and must never be used from both streams at once. The pooler runs on the main stream while the router runs on the side stream; the router does not use the extension, so this holds as written. Do not share one workspace across keys to save memory unless every key is on the main stream.
open_questions: Did the bf16 precedent 26a8be34a5eb4426 compile, capture and pick any non-incumbent algorithm? Its log tail shows this. If load_inline or graph capture failed there, fix the port before claiming. If the TN heuristic returned only near-duplicates of result 0 at m=128/256, expect few picks at T=753, though maybe not at 3012/16384. Claim this hypothesis only after that harvest.

How many candidates does cublasLtMatmulAlgoGetHeuristic return for TN at M=753, 3012 and 16384 with a 32 MiB workspace, and does any of them use stream-K or split-K for the o projection (K=1024)? The o key at turn_1 (39 us vs 12.8 floor) is where a win is most likely.
Should the pooler keys be timed while the router's two mm calls run on the side stream, given that the real graph overlaps them? The answer decides whether a pooler pick is real.
What is the prepare() wall time on top of master's Triton bank compile, Marlin repack and expert checks? Cap max_algos at 16 for the T=16384 keys if it approaches the 300 s limit, and print it.
The first_turn keys are expected flat and cost the most prepare() time. Consider skipping them entirely (T in {753, 3012} only) to cut compile/timing risk, if the precedent shows no picks at large M.
